stories.headline: Dem governor’s tale of mourning fellow serviceman ripped apart after soldier's wife gives brutal fact check
stories.note: Possible 2028 Democratic contender Wes Moore faces fresh questions about his military storytelling, this time from a fallen soldier's widow.
body: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat widely seen as eyeing a 2028 White House bid, is again under fire over how he has described his military service — this time over a story in his 2015 memoir about mourning a fallen fellow soldier.

In the book, Moore wrote that he wept for his friend Tobias "Toby" Meister at his grandfather's funeral. But the Baltimore Sun found the dates don't line up: the funeral was Dec. 17, 2005, and Meister was killed by a roadside bomb 11 days later. Moore reportedly didn't learn of the death until he returned to Afghanistan in January.

Meister's widow, Alicia, told the Sun she had never heard of Moore and didn't recall her husband mentioning him: "I don't know who [Moore] is." After the paper contacted the governor's office, she said Moore called, paid his respects and apologized for not reaching out sooner — but she said she wishes her late husband were kept out of the controversy entirely.

Moore had previously blamed the timeline error on poor editing and the toll of stress and grief on memory. A spokesperson called the latest reporting a "political hit job," said Moore did know and work with Meister, and accused Sinclair's chairman of exploiting a Gold Star family.
The story follows an earlier Sun report in which Moore's former Army supervisor questioned his claim that he led soldiers in combat.

Why it matters: Moore is one of the Democrats' rising national names. A pattern of questions about embellished service stories is the kind of credibility problem that follows a candidate into a presidential primary — and gives Republicans an easy line of attack.

stories.headline: Trump administration permanently pulls funding from LA homeless agency over mounting fraud allegations
stories.note: HUD is cutting LA's scandal-plagued homeless agency off from federal money for good, putting blue-city waste and fraud front and center.
body: The Trump administration announced a settlement that permanently cuts the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) off from federal homelessness funding, citing evidence of fraud and years of mismanagement.

Under the deal, LAHSA gives up about $150 million in federal funds and must fully sever ties with HUD's homelessness programs by the end of 2027. Los Angeles County will take over managing the money, with HUD keeping close watch on how it's spent. The agreement also ends LAHSA's lawsuit over HUD's June funding suspension.

According to HUD, LAHSA took in more federal homelessness money than any other jurisdiction in the country — nearly $1 billion over five years. HUD Secretary Scott Turner said taxpayers "will no longer bankroll an organization that fails to deliver," and federal prosecutor Bill Essayli said complicit groups won't get "one penny more."

HUD also says it is moving away from the "Housing First" model toward "Treatment First," under which people would generally need to take part in addiction or mental health treatment and show progress to keep housing help.
The department pointed to a 6.3% drop in homelessness during Trump's first year back in office, which it called the largest decline on record.

Why it matters: LA's homelessness crisis has long been a symbol of Democratic governance gone wrong. Pulling the plug over fraud lets the administration frame itself as the guardian of taxpayer money and puts the spotlight on how Democrat-run cities spend federal dollars.

stories.headline: White House blasts 'Trumpcare for All' pitch from far-left El-Sayed who called president 'unserious fool'
stories.note: The White House slapped down Sen.-elect El-Sayed's 'Trumpcare for All' stunt, keeping the Democrats' socialist health-care push in the spotlight.
body: Michigan Democrat Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed posted a 16-second video Tuesday urging President Trump to adopt "Trumpcare for All" — essentially Medicare for All with Trump's name on it. The video included a mock "Trumpcare" card and a reference to an AI image depicting Trump as Jesus.

The pitch came shortly after El-Sayed called Trump an "unserious fool" on the "Pod Save America" podcast. In the new video he took a lighter tone, telling Trump the midterms "were rough" and that the plan is popular.
The White House wasn't buying it. Spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the proposal "should really be called 'Medicare for None,'" arguing it would wipe out the coverage Americans rely on.

Schuster instead pointed to Trump's push to make sure Americans don't pay more for prescription drugs than patients in other developed countries, which she said has already saved more than $1 billion. The administration also cited a Council of Economic Advisers estimate that Medicare for All would add roughly $47.4 trillion to deficits from 2027 to 2036 without new taxes, and would shift many people off employer coverage.

Why it matters: Fresh off midterm wins, the Democrats' most progressive new senators are already pushing single-payer health care. Republicans see a government takeover of health insurance — and its massive price tag — as a winning contrast heading into the next fight.

stories.headline: Judge fires back at Fani Willis' office in courtroom clash over Trump case: 'Due process doesn't apply to you'
stories.note: A Georgia appeals panel grilled Fani Willis' office as Trump and co-defendants seek nearly $17 million in legal fees from her collapsed case.
body: A three-judge Georgia appeals panel on Tuesday pressed Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis' office as it asked for the right to fight legal-fee claims from President Trump and other former defendants in her now-dead election interference case.

Trump and his co-defendants are seeking nearly $17 million — more than $6 million for Trump alone — under a new Georgia law that lets defendants recover legal costs when a prosecutor is removed for improper conduct and the charges are later dropped. Willis and her office were disqualified in December 2024 over her romantic relationship with special prosecutor Nathan Wade.

Willis' office argued it needs a seat at the table to protect its budget, saying Pete Skandalakis — the state prosecutors' council director who took over and dismissed the case in November 2025 — can't adequately represent its interests. Judge J. Wade Padgett was blunt: "You're the government. Due process doesn't apply to you."

Judges also asked whether Willis remains "wholly disqualified." Her office's attorney argued the disqualification covered only the criminal prosecution, not the separate fee fight. The panel also raised whether the trial court's finding — an appearance of impropriety, but no proven misconduct — meets the new law's bar for reimbursement.
A lower-court judge had already denied Willis' request to intervene in March, finding Skandalakis could handle the state's side.

Why it matters: The case Democrats once touted as a major threat to Trump has collapsed, and now Willis' office is fighting just to have a say in whether taxpayers cover the defendants' bills — a continuing embarrassment for one of Trump's highest-profile prosecutors.

stories.headline: Dem's campaign promise to freeze energy costs faces glaring reality check
stories.note: Newly elected Democratic governors' promises to 'freeze' power bills are drawing warnings that price controls can't fix supply and could backfire.
body: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, has promised to freeze residential electricity rates on her first day in office using emergency powers — and energy experts are warning the idea may not work in Texas' competitive power market and could even lead to shortages.

She's not alone. Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger wants a six-year rate freeze tied to a proposed utility sale, California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has promised a utility rate freeze, and Ohio Democrats have proposed a 12-month freeze. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill promised an emergency rate cap but has since shifted to bill credits instead.

Sam Romain of the free-market group Americans for Energy Dominance said Democrats "don't have the power to just freeze the rates," calling the plans price controls dressed up as emergencies. He argued a freeze builds nothing and actually discourages developers who can't be sure they'll recoup their investment.
There are legal questions too. Nick Loris of C3 Solutions said there is a lot of skepticism that Texas' disaster law can be stretched to cover a rate freeze.

Why it matters: Affordability helped Democrats win this fall, and energy prices were a big part of that pitch. If their signature fix runs into legal walls or makes supply problems worse, Republicans get a ready-made argument that Democrats over-promised.

stories.headline: Sherrill commits $20.2M to deportation defense while condemning Rutgers over Border Patrol speaker
stories.note: NJ Gov. Sherrill is putting $20.2M toward deportation defense while condemning a Border Patrol speaker at Rutgers, a sharp contrast Republicans are pouncing on.
body: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced $20.2 million for the state's Detention Deportation Defense Initiative — nearly triple its most recent budget — around the same time she criticized Rutgers' College Republicans for hosting retired Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino.
Critics on X said her condemnation helped fuel protests at the New Brunswick event, where demonstrators shouted inside the room and Bovino was briefly led out of the forum.

The money will go to 10 legal service providers representing low-income residents facing detention and deportation, including detainees at Delaney Hall in Essex County. Sherrill said everyone is entitled to due process and accused the Trump administration of creating "impossible obstacles" for people facing deportation.

Republicans pushed back hard. Rep. Jeff Van Drew said New Jersey families are being crushed by high electric bills and property taxes while the governor spends millions defending illegal immigrants, calling it "a complete insult" to taxpayers. A DHS spokesperson said Sherrill has shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens than for victims like Laken Riley and Rachel Morin.

Why it matters: Immigration and cost of living remain two of the GOP's strongest issues. A Democratic governor spending taxpayer money on deportation defense while residents struggle with bills gives Republicans a clear contrast to run on.

stories.headline: House Dems target Trump family, JD Vance in sweeping new investigation push
stories.note: Incoming Oversight Democrats are already launching probes into the Trump family and JD Vance, feeding the GOP argument that they care more about retribution than costs.
body: Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the likely next chairman of the House Oversight Committee, is sending document preservation letters Wednesday to 12 people in President Trump's orbit — before Democrats even take control of the House.

Recipients include Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, Kimberly Guilfoyle and Stephen Miller, plus former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, Corey Lewandowski, Susie Wiles and Attorney General Todd Blanche, among others. Democrats say they plan to probe the Trump family's business dealings, alleged misconduct at DHS and the handling of the Jeffrey Epstein case.
Garcia says the investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation, and his committee would be central to any future impeachment push.

Republicans argue the moves show Democrats are more interested in political retribution than in tackling the cost of living. The Trump family has long denied wrongdoing, and it's unclear whether the targets will comply. Republicans have tapped Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, as their leader and chief spokesman against Democrats' partisan activity.

Why it matters: Democrats won on affordability, but their first big move is a wave of investigations into Trump's family and allies. That gives Republicans a ready-made message heading into 2028: Democrats promised lower costs and delivered subpoenas.
